raw: CHAPTER XVI. Still Knitting
en: [Chapter 16]

raw: Madame Defarge and monsieur her husband returned amicably to the bosom of Saint Antoine, while a speck in a blue cap toiled through the darkness, and through the dust, and down the weary miles of avenue by the wayside, slowly tending towards that point of the compass where the chateau of Monsieur the Marquis, now in his grave, listened to the whispering trees.
en: Still Knitting Madame Defarge and her husband returned to the Saint Antoine neighborhood, while the road mender in his blue cap walked back through the dark and dusty miles toward the castle of the late Marquis.

raw: Such ample leisure had the stone faces, now, for listening to the trees and to the fountain, that the few village scarecrows who, in their quest for herbs to eat and fragments of dead stick to burn, strayed within sight of the great stone courtyard and terrace staircase, had it borne in upon their starved fancy that the expression of the faces was altered.
en: The stone faces on the castle walls had plenty of time now to listen to the wind and the fountain. The few starving peasants who wandered near the courtyard to search for herbs or wood thought the expressions on the stone faces had changed.

raw: A rumour just lived in the village--had a faint and bare existence there, as its people had--that when the knife struck home, the faces changed, from faces of pride to faces of anger and pain; also, that when that dangling figure was hauled up forty feet above the fountain, they changed again, and bore a cruel look of being avenged, which they would henceforth bear for ever.
en: A faint rumor existed in the village. When the Marquis was killed, people said the stone faces changed, from expressions of pride to anger and pain. And when Gaspard was hanged forty feet above the fountain, they changed again.

raw: In the stone face over the great window of the bed-chamber where the murder was done, two fine dints were pointed out in the sculptured nose, which everybody recognised, and which nobody had seen of old; and on the scarce occasions when two or three ragged peasants emerged from the crowd to take a hurried peep at Monsieur the Marquis petrified, a skinny finger would not have pointed to it for a minute, before they all started away among the moss and leaves, like the more fortunate hares who could find a living there.
en: This time, to a cruel look of being avenged. On the stone face over the bedroom window where the murder occurred, two nostrils seemed pinched in a way no one had noticed before. Whenever a few peasants sneaked a look at the stone face, they quickly ran back into the woods like frightened rabbits.

raw: Chateau and hut, stone face and dangling figure, the red stain on the stone floor, and the pure water in the village well--thousands of acres of land--a whole province of France--all France itself--lay under the night sky, concentrated into a faint hair-breadth line. So does a whole world, with all its greatnesses and littlenesses, lie in a twinkling star.
en: The castle and the huts, the stone faces and the hanging body, the bloodstains and the village well, all of France lay under the night sky, looking like a tiny speck from a distance.

raw: And as mere human knowledge can split a ray of light and analyse the manner of its composition, so, sublimer intelligences may read in the feeble shining of this earth of ours, every thought and act, every vice and virtue, of every responsible creature on it.
en: Just as human knowledge can analyze a ray of light, higher minds could read in the earth's light every thought and action of the people on it.

raw: The Defarges, husband and wife, came lumbering under the starlight, in their public vehicle, to that gate of Paris whereunto their journey naturally tended.
en: The Defarges returned in a public carriage to the gates of Paris under the stars.

raw: There was the usual stoppage at the barrier guardhouse, and the usual lanterns came glancing forth for the usual examination and inquiry.
en: The carriage was stopped at the guardhouse for the usual inspection.

raw: Monsieur Defarge alighted; knowing one or two of the soldiery there, and one of the police. The latter he was intimate with, and affectionately embraced.
en: Defarge got out, greeting a few soldiers he knew, and warmly hugging a policeman he was friendly with.

raw: When Saint Antoine had again enfolded the Defarges in his dusky wings, and they, having finally alighted near the Saint’s boundaries, were picking their way on foot through the black mud and offal of his streets, Madame Defarge spoke to her husband:
en: Once they were back in Saint Antoine, walking through the dark, muddy, and garbage-filled streets near its borders, Madame Defarge spoke to her husband:

raw: “Say then, my friend; what did Jacques of the police tell thee?”
en: "Tell me, my friend, what did the policeman tell you?"

raw: “Very little to-night, but all he knows.
en: "Very little tonight, but all he knows.

raw: There is another spy commissioned for our quarter.
en: There is a new spy assigned to our neighborhood.

raw: There may be many more, for all that he can say, but he knows of one.”
en: There might be more, but he only knows of one."

raw: “Eh well!” said Madame Defarge, raising her eyebrows with a cool business air. “It is necessary to register him.
en: "Well," Madame Defarge said with a cool, business-like look, "we must register him.

raw: How do they call that man?”
en: What is his name?"

raw: “He is English.”
en: "He is English."

raw: “So much the better.
en: "So much the better.

raw: His name?”
en: His name?"

raw: “Barsad,” said Defarge, making it French by pronunciation. But, he had been so careful to get it accurately, that he then spelt it with perfect correctness.
en: "Barsad," said Defarge, pronouncing it in a French way, though he spelled it correctly for her.

raw: “Barsad,” repeated madame. “Good.
en: "Barsad," madame repeated. "Good.

raw: Christian name?”
en: First name?"

raw: “John.”
en: "John."

raw: “John Barsad,” repeated madame, after murmuring it once to herself. “Good.
en: "John Barsad," madame repeated, after murmuring it quietly to herself. "Good.

raw: His appearance; is it known?”
en: What does he look like?"

raw: “Age, about forty years; height, about five feet nine; black hair; complexion dark; generally, rather handsome visage; eyes dark, face thin, long, and sallow; nose aquiline, but not straight, having a peculiar inclination towards the left cheek; expression, therefore, sinister.”
en: "About forty years old. About five feet nine inches tall. Black hair. Dark skin. Generally handsome. Thin, long, pale face with dark eyes. His nose is hooked but bends toward his left cheek, giving him a sinister expression."

raw: “Eh my faith.
en: "Well, that is a detailed portrait!" madame laughed.

raw: It is a portrait!” said madame, laughing. “He shall be registered to-morrow.”
en: It is a complete portrait!" madame said with a laugh. "I will knit him into the register tomorrow."

raw: They turned into the wine-shop, which was closed (for it was midnight), and where Madame Defarge immediately took her post at her desk, counted the small moneys that had been taken during her absence, examined the stock, went through the entries in the book, made other entries of her own, checked the serving man in every possible way, and finally dismissed him to bed.
en: They entered their closed shop at midnight. Madame Defarge immediately went to her desk, counted the money taken in their absence, checked the inventory, and went over the ledger entries. She checked the servant's work in every way before sending him to bed.

raw: Then she turned out the contents of the bowl of money for the second time, and began knotting them up in her handkerchief, in a chain of separate knots, for safe keeping through the night.
en: Then she poured the coins out again and began tying them into her handkerchief in a chain of separate knots for safekeeping through the night.

raw: All this while, Defarge, with his pipe in his mouth, walked up and down, complacently admiring, but never interfering; in which condition, indeed, as to the business and his domestic affairs, he walked up and down through life.
en: Defarge smoked his pipe and walked up and down, admiring her work without interfering, which was his habit in both business and family life.

raw: The night was hot, and the shop, close shut and surrounded by so foul a neighbourhood, was ill-smelling.
en: The night was hot, and since the shop was shut tight and surrounded by a dirty neighborhood, it smelled terrible.

raw: Monsieur Defarge’s olfactory sense was by no means delicate, but the stock of wine smelt much stronger than it ever tasted, and so did the stock of rum and brandy and aniseed.
en: The closed shop smelled of the dirty neighborhood, mixed with the strong smell of wine, rum, and brandy.

raw: He whiffed the compound of scents away, as he put down his smoked-out pipe.
en: Defarge put down his pipe and fanned the air.

raw: “You are fatigued,” said madame, raising her glance as she knotted the money. “There are only the usual odours.”
en: "You are tired," madame said, looking up from her knots. "It is just the usual smells."

raw: “I am a little tired,” her husband acknowledged.
en: "I am a little tired," her husband admitted.

raw: “You are a little depressed, too,” said madame, whose quick eyes had never been so intent on the accounts, but they had had a ray or two for him. “Oh, the men, the men!”
en: "You seem a bit depressed, too," said madame. Even while closely checking the accounts, her sharp eyes always kept a watch on him. "Oh, you men, you men!"

raw: “But my dear!” began Defarge.
en: "But my dear!" Defarge began.

raw: “But my dear!” repeated madame, nodding firmly; “but my dear!
en: "But my dear!" madame repeated firmly.

raw: You are faint of heart to-night, my dear!”
en: "You are weak-hearted tonight, my dear!"

raw: “Well, then,” said Defarge, as if a thought were wrung out of his breast, “it _is_ a long time.”
en: "Well," Defarge said, sighing, "it _is_ taking a long time."

raw: “It is a long time,” repeated his wife; “and when is it not a long time?
en: "It takes a long time," his wife repeated.

raw: Vengeance and retribution require a long time; it is the rule.”
en: "Vengeance always takes a long time; that is the rule."

raw: “It does not take a long time to strike a man with Lightning,” said Defarge.
en: "It doesn't take long for lightning to strike," said Defarge.

raw: “How long,” demanded madame, composedly, “does it take to make and store the lightning?
en: Madame asked calmly, "How long does it take to make and store the lightning?

raw: Tell me.”
en: Tell me."

raw: Defarge raised his head thoughtfully, as if there were something in that too.
en: Defarge raised his head thoughtfully, as if her words had some truth to them.

raw: “It does not take a long time,” said madame, “for an earthquake to swallow a town.
en: Madame said, "It doesn't take long for an earthquake to destroy a town.

raw: Eh well! Tell me how long it takes to prepare the earthquake?”
en: But tell me how long it takes to prepare the earthquake?"

raw: “A long time, I suppose,” said Defarge.
en: "A long time, I suppose," said Defarge.

raw: “But when it is ready, it takes place, and grinds to pieces everything before it.
en: "But when it is ready, it happens and crushes everything.

raw: In the meantime, it is always preparing, though it is not seen or heard.
en: Meanwhile, it is always preparing, even if it is quiet.

raw: That is your consolation. Keep it.”
en: Remember that."

raw: She tied a knot with flashing eyes, as if it throttled a foe.
en: She tied a tight knot as if strangling an enemy.

raw: “I tell thee,” said madame, extending her right hand, for emphasis, “that although it is a long time on the road, it is on the road and coming.
en: "I am telling you," madame said, stretching out her right hand for emphasis, "that even though it has been a long time coming, it is still on its way.

raw: I tell thee it never retreats, and never stops. I tell thee it is always advancing.
en: It is taking a long time, yes, but it never stops or retreats.

raw: Look around and consider the lives of all the world that we know, consider the faces of all the world that we know, consider the rage and discontent to which the Jacquerie addresses itself with more and more of certainty every hour.
en: Look around at the lives and faces of everyone we know. Think about the anger and frustration that our secret movement is building upon, growing more certain every single hour.

raw: Can such things last?
en: Can the nobles last?

raw: Bah!
en: Bah!

raw: I mock you.”
en: I laugh at your doubts."

raw: “My brave wife,” returned Defarge, standing before her with his head a little bent, and his hands clasped at his back, like a docile and attentive pupil before his catechist, “I do not question all this.
en: "My brave wife," Defarge said, standing before her with his hands behind his back like an attentive student, "I do not doubt it.

raw: But it has lasted a long time, and it is possible--you know well, my wife, it is possible--that it may not come, during our lives.”
en: But it has lasted a long time, and it is possible that the victory won't come during our lives."

raw: “Eh well! How then?” demanded madame, tying another knot, as if there were another enemy strangled.
en: "Well, what of it?" madame asked, tying another tight knot.

raw: “Well!” said Defarge, with a half complaining and half apologetic shrug. “We shall not see the triumph.”
en: "Well," Defarge said, shrugging, "we won't see the victory."

raw: “We shall have helped it,” returned madame, with her extended hand in strong action. “Nothing that we do, is done in vain.
en: "We will have helped bring it about," madame replied, waving her hand. "Nothing we do is in vain.

raw: I believe, with all my soul, that we shall see the triumph.
en: I believe we will see the victory.

raw: But even if not, even if I knew certainly not, show me the neck of an aristocrat and tyrant, and still I would--”
en: But even if we don't, if I were shown a tyrant's neck, I would still, "

raw: Then madame, with her teeth set, tied a very terrible knot indeed.
en: Madame set her teeth and tied a very tight, terrible knot.

raw: “Hold!” cried Defarge, reddening a little as if he felt charged with cowardice; “I too, my dear, will stop at nothing.”
en: "Hold on!" cried Defarge, turning a little red, as if he felt she was calling him a coward. "I too, my dear, will stop at nothing."

raw: “Yes!
en: "Yes!

raw: But it is your weakness that you sometimes need to see your victim and your opportunity, to sustain you.
en: But you are weak because you need to see the victim and the opportunity to keep your courage up.

raw: Sustain yourself without that.
en: You must stay strong without that.

raw: When the time comes, let loose a tiger and a devil; but wait for the time with the tiger and the devil chained--not shown--yet always ready.”
en: When the time comes, act like a tiger; but wait for the time with the tiger chained and hidden, yet always ready."

raw: Madame enforced the conclusion of this piece of advice by striking her little counter with her chain of money as if she knocked its brains out, and then gathering the heavy handkerchief under her arm in a serene manner, and observing that it was time to go to bed.
en: Madame hit the counter with her chain of money to emphasize her point, then calmly gathered her handkerchief and said it was time for bed.

raw: Next noontide saw the admirable woman in her usual place in the wine-shop, knitting away assiduously.
en: The next noon found Madame Defarge at her usual place, knitting.

raw: A rose lay beside her, and if she now and then glanced at the flower, it was with no infraction of her usual preoccupied air.
en: A rose lay beside her, and although she glanced at it now and then, she never lost her focused, busy appearance.

raw: There were a few customers, drinking or not drinking, standing or seated, sprinkled about.
en: A few customers were in the shop.

raw: The day was very hot, and heaps of flies, who were extending their inquisitive and adventurous perquisitions into all the glutinous little glasses near madame, fell dead at the bottom.
en: The day was very hot, and swarms of flies died at the bottom of the sticky glasses near madame.

raw: Their decease made no impression on the other flies out promenading, who looked at them in the coolest manner (as if they themselves were elephants, or something as far removed), until they met the same fate. Curious to consider how heedless flies are!--perhaps they thought as much at Court that sunny summer day.
en: Their deaths made no impression on the other flying bugs, who coolly ignored them as if they were entirely different creatures—until they met the same fate. It's funny how careless flies are; perhaps the people at the Royal Court thought the exact same way on that sunny summer day.

raw: A figure entering at the door threw a shadow on Madame Defarge which she felt to be a new one.
en: A figure entering the door cast a new shadow over Madame Defarge.

raw: She laid down her knitting, and began to pin her rose in her head-dress, before she looked at the figure.
en: Before looking up, she laid down her knitting and pinned the rose into her headdress.

raw: It was curious. The moment Madame Defarge took up the rose, the customers ceased talking, and began gradually to drop out of the wine-shop.
en: It was strange: the moment Madame Defarge pinned the rose, the customers stopped talking and gradually left the shop.

raw: “Good day, madame,” said the new-comer.
en: "Good day, madame," said the newcomer.

raw: “Good day, monsieur.”
en: "Good day, monsieur."

raw: She said it aloud, but added to herself, as she resumed her knitting: “Hah!
en: She said this out loud, but as she went back to her knitting, she added to herself: "Hah!

raw: Good day, age about forty, height about five feet nine, black hair, generally rather handsome visage, complexion dark, eyes dark, thin, long and sallow face, aquiline nose but not straight, having a peculiar inclination towards the left cheek which imparts a sinister expression!
en: But silently, she added to herself: "John Barsad. Age about forty. Height about five feet nine. Black hair. Handsome but pale face.

raw: Good day, one and all!”
en: Dark eyes. Hooked nose bending left. Sinister look. Good day, spy!"

raw: “Have the goodness to give me a little glass of old cognac, and a mouthful of cool fresh water, madame.”
en: "Please give me a glass of cognac and some fresh water, madame."

raw: Madame complied with a polite air.
en: Madame served him politely.

raw: “Marvellous cognac this, madame!”
en: "Excellent cognac, madame!"

raw: It was the first time it had ever been so complimented, and Madame Defarge knew enough of its antecedents to know better.
en: It was the first time anyone had complimented the cheap cognac, and Madame Defarge knew its poor quality well.

raw: She said, however, that the cognac was flattered, and took up her knitting.
en: She replied that the cognac was flattered and went back to her knitting.

raw: The visitor watched her fingers for a few moments, and took the opportunity of observing the place in general.
en: The visitor watched her fingers for a moment and looked around the shop.

raw: “You knit with great skill, madame.”
en: "You knit very well, madame."

raw: “I am accustomed to it.”
en: "I am used to it."

raw: “A pretty pattern too!”
en: "A pretty pattern too!"

raw: “_You_ think so?” said madame, looking at him with a smile.
en: "Do _you_ think so?" madame asked with a smile.

raw: “Decidedly.
en: "Definitely.

raw: May one ask what it is for?”
en: May I ask what it is for?"

raw: “Pastime,” said madame, still looking at him with a smile while her fingers moved nimbly.
en: "A pastime," madame replied, her fingers moving quickly.

raw: “Not for use?”
en: "Not for use?"

raw: “That depends.
en: "That depends.

raw: I may find a use for it one day.
en: I might find a use for it one day.

raw: If I do--Well,” said madame, drawing a breath and nodding her head with a stern kind of coquetry, “I’ll use it!”
en: And if I do find him—well," madame said, taking a breath and giving a stern, flirtatious nod, "I'll use it!"

raw: It was remarkable; but, the taste of Saint Antoine seemed to be decidedly opposed to a rose on the head-dress of Madame Defarge.
en: It was remarkable, but the customers clearly did not like the rose in Madame Defarge's hair.

raw: Two men had entered separately, and had been about to order drink, when, catching sight of that novelty, they faltered, made a pretence of looking about as if for some friend who was not there, and went away.
en: Two men who entered to buy drinks saw the rose, hesitated, pretended to look for someone, and walked out.

raw: Nor, of those who had been there when this visitor entered, was there one left.
en: Soon the shop was empty of all previous customers.

raw: They had all dropped off. The spy had kept his eyes open, but had been able to detect no sign.
en: The spy watched closely but saw no signs of plotting.

raw: They had lounged away in a poverty-stricken, purposeless, accidental manner, quite natural and unimpeachable.
en: The customers had left in a natural, casual way.

raw: “_John_,” thought madame, checking off her work as her fingers knitted, and her eyes looked at the stranger. “Stay long enough, and I shall knit ‘BARSAD’ before you go.”
en: "John," madame thought, her fingers knitting. "Stay long enough, and I will knit 'BARSAD' before you go."

raw: “You have a husband, madame?”
en: "Do you have a husband, madame?"

raw: “I have.”
en: "I do."

raw: “Children?”
en: "Children?"

raw: “No children.”
en: "No children."

raw: “Business seems bad?”
en: "Business seems poor?"

raw: “Business is very bad; the people are so poor.”
en: "Business is very poor; the people are starving."

raw: “Ah, the unfortunate, miserable people!
en: "Ah, the poor, oppressed people!

raw: So oppressed, too--as you say.”
en: As you say."

raw: “As _you_ say,” madame retorted, correcting him, and deftly knitting an extra something into his name that boded him no good.
en: "As _you_ say," madame corrected him, knitting his name into her register.

raw: “Pardon me; certainly it was I who said so, but you naturally think so. Of course.”
en: "Forgive me; yes, I said it, but you must think so too."

raw: “_I_ think?” returned madame, in a high voice. “I and my husband have enough to do to keep this wine-shop open, without thinking.
en: "Me, think?" madame replied in a loud voice. "My husband and I have enough work just keeping this wine-shop open, without having time to think.

raw: All we think, here, is how to live.
en: "My husband and I have enough work keeping this shop open without thinking.

raw: That is the subject _we_ think of, and it gives us, from morning to night, enough to think about, without embarrassing our heads concerning others. _I_ think for others?
en: That is all we think about, and it keeps us busy from morning to night without worrying about other people. You expect me to think about others?

raw: No, no.”
en: That keeps us busy enough without worrying about others."

raw: The spy, who was there to pick up any crumbs he could find or make, did not allow his baffled state to express itself in his sinister face; but, stood with an air of gossiping gallantry, leaning his elbow on Madame Defarge’s little counter, and occasionally sipping his cognac.
en: The spy, who was there to gather any bit of information he could, hid his confusion behind his wicked face. Instead, he stood there looking like a polite gossip, leaning his elbow on Madame Defarge's small counter and occasionally sipping his cognac.

raw: “A bad business this, madame, of Gaspard’s execution.
en: "A terrible thing, Gaspard's execution," he sighed.

raw: Ah! the poor Gaspard!” With a sigh of great compassion.
en: Ah! Poor Gaspard!" he added, with a sigh full of fake pity.

raw: “My faith!” returned madame, coolly and lightly, “if people use knives for such purposes, they have to pay for it.
en: Madame replied coldly, "Well, if people use knives to kill, they must pay the price.

raw: He knew beforehand what the price of his luxury was; he has paid the price.”
en: He knew the cost; he has paid it."

raw: “I believe,” said the spy, dropping his soft voice to a tone that invited confidence, and expressing an injured revolutionary susceptibility in every muscle of his wicked face: “I believe there is much compassion and anger in this neighbourhood, touching the poor fellow?
en: "I believe," the spy whispered, dropping his voice to sound trustworthy and making his wicked face look like a hurt revolutionary's, "I believe there is a lot of sympathy and anger in this neighborhood for the poor man?"

raw: Between ourselves.”
en: Just between us."

raw: “Is there?” asked madame, vacantly.
en: "Is there?" madame asked blankly.

raw: “Is there not?”
en: "Is there not?"

raw: “--Here is my husband!” said Madame Defarge.
en: "Here is my husband," Madame Defarge said.

raw: As the keeper of the wine-shop entered at the door, the spy saluted him by touching his hat, and saying, with an engaging smile, “Good day, Jacques!” Defarge stopped short, and stared at him.
en: As Defarge entered, the spy touched his hat and said with a smile, "Good day, Jacques!" Defarge stopped and stared at him.

raw: “Good day, Jacques!” the spy repeated; with not quite so much confidence, or quite so easy a smile under the stare.
en: "Good day, Jacques!" the spy repeated, his smile faltering under the stare.

raw: “You deceive yourself, monsieur,” returned the keeper of the wine-shop. “You mistake me for another.
en: "You are fooling yourself, monsieur," replied the wine-shop owner. "You are mistaking me for someone else.

raw: That is not my name.
en: "That is not my name.

raw: I am Ernest Defarge.”
en: I am Ernest Defarge."

raw: “It is all the same,” said the spy, airily, but discomfited too: “good day!”
en: "It's all the same," the spy said quickly. "Good day!"

raw: “Good day!” answered Defarge, drily.
en: "Good day," Defarge replied dryly.

raw: “I was saying to madame, with whom I had the pleasure of chatting when you entered, that they tell me there is--and no wonder!--much sympathy and anger in Saint Antoine, touching the unhappy fate of poor Gaspard.”
en: "I was just saying to madame that I hear there is much sympathy and anger in Saint Antoine over Gaspard's death."

raw: “No one has told me so,” said Defarge, shaking his head. “I know nothing of it.”
en: "No one has told me so," said Defarge. "I know nothing about it."

raw: Having said it, he passed behind the little counter, and stood with his hand on the back of his wife’s chair, looking over that barrier at the person to whom they were both opposed, and whom either of them would have shot with the greatest satisfaction.
en: After saying this, he walked behind the little counter and stood with his hand on the back of his wife’s chair. He stared over the counter at the man they both hated, someone either of them would have gladly shot dead.

raw: The spy, well used to his business, did not change his unconscious attitude, but drained his little glass of cognac, took a sip of fresh water, and asked for another glass of cognac.
en: The spy, who was used to this kind of work, kept up his careless attitude. He finished his small glass of cognac, took a sip of water, and ordered another cognac.

raw: Madame Defarge poured it out for him, took to her knitting again, and hummed a little song over it.
en: Madame Defarge poured it, went back to her knitting, and began humming a tune.

raw: “You seem to know this quarter well; that is to say, better than I do?”  observed Defarge.
en: "You seem to know this neighborhood well, better than I do?" Defarge remarked.

raw: “Not at all, but I hope to know it better.
en: "Not at all, but I hope to know it better.

raw: I am so profoundly interested in its miserable inhabitants.”
en: I am very interested in these poor people."

raw: “Hah!” muttered Defarge.
en: "Ah," Defarge muttered.

raw: “The pleasure of conversing with you, Monsieur Defarge, recalls to me,”  pursued the spy, “that I have the honour of cherishing some interesting associations with your name.”
en: The spy continued, "Monsieur Defarge, speaking with you reminds me of something. I have some interesting associations with your name."

raw: “Indeed!” said Defarge, with much indifference.
en: "Indeed?" Defarge said indifferently.

raw: “Yes, indeed.
en: "Yes.

raw: When Doctor Manette was released, you, his old domestic, had the charge of him, I know.
en: When Doctor Manette was released, you, as his old servant, took care of him.

raw: He was delivered to you.
en: He was delivered to you.

raw: You see I am informed of the circumstances?”
en: You see I know the details?"

raw: “Such is the fact, certainly,” said Defarge.
en: "That is true," said Defarge.

raw: He had had it conveyed to him, in an accidental touch of his wife’s elbow as she knitted and warbled, that he would do best to answer, but always with brevity.
en: Through an accidental bump from his wife's elbow as she knitted and hummed, she had silently warned him that it was best to answer, but to keep it short.

raw: “It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and it was from your care that his daughter took him, accompanied by a neat brown monsieur; how is he called?--in a little wig--Lorry--of the bank of Tellson and Company--over to England.”
en: The spy said, "It was to you that his daughter came, and you delivered him to her and that banker in the wig, Lorry, who took them to England."

raw: “Such is the fact,” repeated Defarge. “Very interesting remembrances!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter, in England.”
en: "That is true," Defarge repeated. "I knew Doctor Manette and his daughter in England," the spy said.

raw: “Yes?” said Defarge.
en: "Yes?"

raw: “You don’t hear much about them now?” said the spy.
en: "You don't hear from them now?"

raw: “No,” said Defarge.
en: "No," said Defarge.

raw: “In effect,” madame struck in, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear about them.
en: "In fact," madame interrupted, looking up, "we never hear from them.

raw: We received the news of their safe arrival, and perhaps another letter, or perhaps two; but, since then, they have gradually taken their road in life--we, ours--and we have held no correspondence.”
en: We heard they arrived safely, and maybe got a letter or two after that. But since then, they've gone their way and we've gone ours, and we haven't kept in touch."

raw: “Perfectly so, madame,” replied the spy. “She is going to be married.”
en: "I see," the spy said. "She is going to be married."

raw: “Going?” echoed madame. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago.
en: "Married?" madame echoed. "She was pretty enough to marry long ago.

raw: You English are cold, it seems to me.”
en: You English are very cold."

raw: “Oh!
en: "Oh!

raw: You know I am English.”
en: You know I am English."

raw: “I perceive your tongue is,” returned madame; “and what the tongue is, I suppose the man is.”
en: "I can tell by your accent," madame replied. "A man is what his tongue is."

raw: He did not take the identification as a compliment; but he made the best of it, and turned it off with a laugh.
en: He did not take it as a compliment but laughed it off.

raw: After sipping his cognac to the end, he added:
en: He finished his drink and added:

raw: “Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married.
en: "Yes, Miss Manette is marrying.

raw: But not to an Englishman; to one who, like herself, is French by birth. And speaking of Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard!
en: But she's not marrying an Englishman; she's marrying someone born in France, just like her. And speaking of Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard!

raw: It was cruel, cruel!), it is a curious thing that she is going to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was exalted to that height of so many feet; in other words, the present Marquis.
en: And speaking of Gaspard, it is a strange coincidence: she is marrying the nephew of the Marquis whom Gaspard killed.

raw: But he lives unknown in England, he is no Marquis there; he is Mr.
en: But he lives secretly in England, where he isn't called a Marquis; he is Mr.

raw: Charles Darnay.
en: But he lives quietly in England under the name Charles Darnay.

raw: D’Aulnais is the name of his mother’s family.”
en: D'Aulnais is his mother's family name."

raw: Madame Defarge knitted steadily, but the intelligence had a palpable effect upon her husband.
en: Madame Defarge knitted steadily, but the news clearly upset her husband.

raw: Do what he would, behind the little counter, as to the striking of a light and the lighting of his pipe, he was troubled, and his hand was not trustworthy.
en: No matter how hard he tried to hide it behind the counter, he was deeply troubled as he struck a match, and his hand shook unsteadily while lighting his pipe.

raw: The spy would have been no spy if he had failed to see it, or to record it in his mind.
en: The spy noticed his reaction and recorded it in his mind.

raw: Having made, at least, this one hit, whatever it might prove to be worth, and no customers coming in to help him to any other, Mr.
en: Having finally landed this one hit, whatever it was worth, and with no other customers coming in to give him more clues, Mr.

raw: Barsad paid for what he had drunk, and took his leave: taking occasion to say, in a genteel manner, before he departed, that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again.
en: Barsad paid for his drinks and left. Before walking out, he made sure to say in a polite tone that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again.

raw: For some minutes after he had emerged into the outer presence of Saint Antoine, the husband and wife remained exactly as he had left them, lest he should come back.
en: For a few minutes after he stepped out into the streets of Saint Antoine, the husband and wife stood completely still in case he decided to come back.

raw: “Can it be true,” said Defarge, in a low voice, looking down at his wife as he stood smoking with his hand on the back of her chair: “what he has said of Ma’amselle Manette?”
en: "Can it be true," Defarge said in a low voice, looking down at his wife as he smoked with his hand on the back of her chair, "what he said about Miss Manette?"

raw: “As he has said it,” returned madame, lifting her eyebrows a little, “it is probably false.
en: Madame replied, "Since he said it, it is probably a lie.

raw: But it may be true.”
en: But it might be true."

raw: “If it is--” Defarge began, and stopped.
en: "If it is, " Defarge began.

raw: “If it is?” repeated his wife.
en: "If it is?"

raw: “--And if it does come, while we live to see it triumph--I hope, for her sake, Destiny will keep her husband out of France.”
en: ", and if the revolution comes in our lifetime, I hope for her sake that her husband stays out of France."

raw: “Her husband’s destiny,” said Madame Defarge, with her usual composure, “will take him where he is to go, and will lead him to the end that is to end him.
en: Madame Defarge said calmly, "Her husband’s destiny will take him where he must go, and lead him to his end.

raw: That is all I know.”
en: That is all."

raw: “But it is very strange--now, at least, is it not very strange”--said Defarge, rather pleading with his wife to induce her to admit it, “that, after all our sympathy for Monsieur her father, and herself, her husband’s name should be proscribed under your hand at this moment, by the side of that infernal dog’s who has just left us?”
en: "But it is very strange," Defarge said, wanting his wife to agree. "After all our sympathy for the Doctor and his daughter, her husband's name is now registered for death by your hand, right next to the name of that spy who just left?"

raw: “Stranger things than that will happen when it does come,” answered madame. “I have them both here, of a certainty; and they are both here for their merits; that is enough.”
en: "Stranger things will happen when the revolution comes," madame answered. "They are both on the list for their actions, and that is enough."

raw: She rolled up her knitting when she had said those words, and presently took the rose out of the handkerchief that was wound about her head.
en: She rolled up her knitting and took the rose out of her hair.

raw: Either Saint Antoine had an instinctive sense that the objectionable decoration was gone, or Saint Antoine was on the watch for its disappearance; howbeit, the Saint took courage to lounge in, very shortly afterwards, and the wine-shop recovered its habitual aspect.
en: The neighborhood people, seeing the rose was gone, began coming back into the shop, and it returned to its usual state.

raw: In the evening, at which season of all others Saint Antoine turned himself inside out, and sat on door-steps and window-ledges, and came to the corners of vile streets and courts, for a breath of air, Madame Defarge with her work in her hand was accustomed to pass from place to place and from group to group: a Missionary--there were many like her--such as the world will do well never to breed again.
en: In the evening, when the people of Saint Antoine came out to sit on their doorsteps, window-ledges, and street corners just to get a breath of fresh air, Madame Defarge would walk from group to group with her knitting. She acted like a dark missionary, spreading her message—one of many like her, whom the world would do well never to create again.

raw: All the women knitted.
en: She was like a missionary of anger, and all the women knitted with her.

raw: They knitted worthless things; but, the mechanical work was a mechanical substitute for eating and drinking; the hands moved for the jaws and the digestive apparatus: if the bony fingers had been still, the stomachs would have been more famine-pinched.
en: They knitted useless things, but the repetitive work was a substitute for eating and drinking. Their moving hands distracted from their empty stomachs; if their bony fingers had stopped, the pain of hunger would have felt even sharper.

raw: But, as the fingers went, the eyes went, and the thoughts.
en: As they knitted, their eyes and thoughts moved quickly.

raw: And as Madame Defarge moved on from group to group, all three went quicker and fiercer among every little knot of women that she had spoken with, and left behind.
en: And as Madame Defarge moved from group to group, the knitting, the dark thoughts, and the desire for revenge grew faster and fiercer among the knots of women she spoke with and left behind.

raw: Her husband smoked at his door, looking after her with admiration. “A great woman,” said he, “a strong woman, a grand woman, a frightfully grand woman!”
en: Her husband watched her with admiration. "A great, strong, and terrifying woman!" he muttered.

raw: Darkness closed around, and then came the ringing of church bells and the distant beating of the military drums in the Palace Courtyard, as the women sat knitting, knitting.
en: Darkness fell all around, followed by the ringing of church bells and the distant beating of military drums in the Palace Courtyard, all while the women just sat there, knitting and knitting.

raw: Darkness encompassed them.
en: The women sat knitting in the dark.

raw: Another darkness was closing in as surely, when the church bells, then ringing pleasantly in many an airy steeple over France, should be melted into thundering cannon; when the military drums should be beating to drown a wretched voice, that night all potent as the voice of Power and Plenty, Freedom and Life.
en: A greater darkness was coming over France, when these church bells would be melted into cannons, and the drums would beat to drown out the screams of the dying.

raw: So much was closing in about the women who sat knitting, knitting, that they their very selves were closing in around a structure yet unbuilt, where they were to sit knitting, knitting, counting dropping heads.
en: The women sat knitting, preparing for the day when they would sit by the guillotine, counting the falling heads.
